free_tier.stated: Quoted: 'The following runners are available on Codeberg. The specs are guidelines for how many resources builds are allowed to take at most, but we rely on "fair use".' The table is codeberg-tiny 1 CPU / 2G / 2 min, codeberg-small 2 CPU / 4G / 5 min, codeberg-medium 4 CPU / 8G / 10 min, all amd64. No monthly quota is published: the constraint is a per-job runtime ceiling of 10 minutes on the largest runner, plus a fair-use clause. Quoted: 'Currently, we put strict resource and time constraints on hosted Forgejo Actions runs, because we do not have an approval workflow like in our hosted Woodpecker CI/CD.'
free_tier.notes: there is no published monthly allowance; the unit of consumption is a job, capped at 10 minutes on the best runner

interface_detail: inferred from the tooling the provider documents; not probed
chaining: Useful only as a lint-and-check lane beside a real build host: ten minutes of 4 vCPU is enough to run a formatter, a type check or a small unit suite, and the repository hosting is free beside it.

limits.value: 10 minutes of wall clock on codeberg-medium, the largest runner, which is 4 CPU and 8G. codeberg-small is 5 minutes and codeberg-tiny is 2 minutes. Quoted: 'The specs are guidelines for how many resources builds are allowed to take at most, but we rely on "fair use".'

The RAM allocation counts filesystem writes against it: 'If your software uses 1 GB of RAM and wrote 1 GB of temporary files, it will be counted as 2 GB against the quota.' 2 GB of extra temp storage per container is granted.
The queue is shared and its fairness is enforced socially, not by a number: 'Don't jam the queue so other projects can also benefit from our offer.'
A '-lazy' variant of each runner trades latency for scheduling: 'We aim for completing the job within 24 hours'

limits_note: The 10-minute per-job ceiling on codeberg-medium binds first and it binds absolutely: no amount of queue patience makes a 30-minute job run. There is no published monthly allowance, so the ceiling is per job and the aggregate is fair use, which is a discretionary throttle rather than a quota.
binding_note: the 10-minute wall clock on the largest runner fails first and it fails hard: 4 vCPU for 10 minutes is 0.67 vCPU-hours per job, so a job that needs more than ten minutes cannot run at all however idle the queue is.

identity_cost.detail: Quoted: 'fill in your username and email address and then choose a good password' and 'After confirming your email address by clicking the link in the email we sent you, you're done and go to go.' No card, no hold, no phone and no identity document. Forgejo Actions needs no approval step, unlike Woodpecker: 'we do not have an approval workflow like in our hosted Woodpecker CI/CD'.

reliability_note: Codeberg's own documentation says of the CI service: 'CI access is provided as-is and might break at any time and for an undefined period of time, due to server issues, for testing and maintenance purposes or human error.' Hosted Forgejo Actions is described as 'open alpha'.

notes: The smallest compute ceiling, and the record is worth keeping precisely because it is small: 0.67 vCPU-hours per job against GitHub's 24 vCPU-hours, a factor of 36. Two things make it worse than the arithmetic suggests for a user. First, there is no published monthly allowance, so the aggregate is 'fair use', which is a discretionary throttle with no threshold to design against. Second, Codeberg's rules name the exact use this corpus exists to serve: 'No extensive pipelines to assist LLM-driven workflows'. What the record does is state the sentence. Not established: the egress term; whether the container is destroyed at job end (the 2 GB per-container temp storage grant implies it, but no sentence says so); and whether a job queued on a lazy runner counts against any aggregate at all, because no aggregate is published.

shape.note: codeberg-medium, the largest published runner: '4 | 8G | 10 min'. Disk is not published; the page grants '2 GB of additional storage for temporary files per container' and warns that filesystem writes count against the RAM allocation.

extras.price_arithmetic: USD 0.00, and no arithmetic is possible: there is no published monthly allowance. One job on codeberg-medium is 4 vCPU x 10 min = 0.67 vCPU-hours. The aggregate depends on how many jobs the fair-use policy tolerates, which is not a number and so cannot be multiplied. This is the corpus's documented-absence rule: 'unlimited' may not be inferred from the silence, and neither may a daily total.
